analysis.investment_thesis: Apollo Micro Systems operates in the right sector — India's defense indigenization is a decade-long tailwind — but at 113x P/E with a 10% ROE and chronically negative free cash flow, you are paying a champagne price for a lassi-quality balance sheet. The business consumes capital; it does not generate it.
key_strengths: Defense indigenization tailwind: India's defense capex and 'Make in India' mandate give structural order-book visibility for domestic suppliers like AMSL.
Revenue growing at 18% CAGR (FY20–25) with net profit accelerating to 32% CAGR — execution on the top line is real.
Manageable D/E of 0.33 — balance sheet leverage is not yet dangerous, though borrowings have grown 4x from INR 83 Cr to INR 361 Cr.
key_risks: Egregious valuation: 113x trailing P/E, 58x EV/EBITDA — even the forward P/E of 65x leaves zero margin of safety; a 10% ROE business deserves 20-25x, not 100x+.
Persistently negative FCF: Free cash flow was -131 Cr (FY24) and -82 Cr (FY25); OCF was positive in only 3 of 5 years — growth is funded by equity dilution and debt, not operations.
Revenue concentration risk: Near-total dependence on government defense contracts with no meaningful private or export diversification — a budget delay or order cancellation can crater the P&L.
red_flags: Massive equity dilution in FY2025: Reserves jumped INR 556 Cr (490→1,046 Cr) against net profit of only INR 56 Cr — a large QIP was done, diluting existing shareholders substantially.
ROE of 10% is far below my 15% minimum threshold — the company is not earning adequately on the capital entrusted to it.
Business almost entirely dependent on government contracts — a hard red flag in my framework with no private sector or export revenue buffer.
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Apollo Micro Systems is a Hyderabad-based defense electronics company building everything from missile interface units to UAV jammers — genuinely exciting products riding India's defense indigenization wave. Revenue grew from INR 246 Cr (FY20) to INR 562 Cr (FY25) at an 18% CAGR and net profit from INR 14 Cr to INR 56 Cr at a 32% CAGR. These are real numbers. But here is what the market is ignoring: the business is a capital furnace. Free cash flow has been negative in four of the last five years, peaking at -131 Cr in FY24. Operating CF turned barely positive at INR 10 Cr in FY25 only after the company raised hundreds of crores via a dilutive equity issuance — reserves ballooned INR 556 Cr against a profit of only INR 56 Cr. That is not organic strength; that is survival financing dressed up as growth.

At INR 10,639 Cr market cap on INR 56 Cr net profit, the market is pricing in flawless execution for the next decade. I have seen this movie before — small defense companies get re-rated on India's defense budget headlines, then reality bites when orders slip, working capital balloons, and promoters quietly place shares. ROE of 10% tells the real story: for every rupee of equity deployed, this business earns 10 paise. My threshold is 15%, and my best ideas earn 20-25%. The defense story is real — I would love to own a well-priced, cash-generating defense champion — but Apollo Micro at 113x P/E with chronically negative FCF and a freshly diluted equity base is not that company today. Wait for the business to prove consistent positive FCF for two consecutive years and for the market to correct to a rational 25-35x earnings. Only then should one revisit.
